coverage: Nine stories · AI, privacy, chips, wearables, networks, space, climate and student engineering

cards.headline: AI glasses raise a new question: who is recording?
cards.summary: Smart glasses and other AI wearables can see, hear and respond to the world around them, but their always-ready cameras and microphones are creating privacy concerns. Reuters reports that some venues have restricted Meta's Ray-Ban glasses while courts and users debate recording, consent and anonymity.
cards.whyItMatters: Wearable computers blur the line between using technology and collecting data about everyone nearby. Designing useful devices also means deciding how people can tell when sensors are active and what happens to the data.

csp.connection: Computing devices can affect people who are not using them, raising questions about privacy, consent and data collection.

cards.headline: Banks warn AI shopping bots can create new risks
cards.summary: A group of banks says AI agents that shop for people could increase scams, fraud, mistaken purchases and data-privacy problems. They want clearer rules for how shopping agents handle card details, explain decisions and identify themselves when making transactions.
cards.whyItMatters: An AI that recommends a product is different from one allowed to spend your money. Giving software permission to act for you makes authentication, privacy and error handling much more important.

csp.connection: Automated systems can make decisions and take actions for users, creating new questions about security, responsibility and control.

cards.headline: Alibaba pairs a new AI chip with a much bigger model
cards.summary: Alibaba unveiled its Zhenwu V900 AI processor and said it plans to train a model with 5 trillion to 10 trillion parameters. The company says the chip can connect in very large clusters; it expects mass production and commercial release in early 2027.
cards.whyItMatters: Modern AI is a software-and-hardware problem at the same time. Larger models need huge amounts of computation, so the design of chips and the networks connecting them can shape what AI systems are practical.

csp.connection: Large computing tasks depend on processors and networks working together as a system.

cards.headline: Poll finds Americans want more attention on AI safety
cards.summary: A Reuters/Ipsos poll of 1,277 U.S. adults found 73% were worried AI companies had not done enough to prevent serious societal harm. The same share said safe, responsible AI development was more important than keeping the U.S. ahead of other countries; the poll's margin of error was about 3 points.
cards.whyItMatters: People affected by computing systems do not always view progress the same way developers do. Polling is one kind of data that can help explain how the public weighs new capabilities against possible risks.

csp.connection: Survey data can be collected and analyzed to understand how groups of people view computing innovations.

cards.headline: Oura's smart ring business heads toward the stock market
cards.summary: Oura began the process of selling shares to the public, putting a spotlight on a wearable built around continuous health and activity sensing. The company's ring turns measurements from tiny sensors into data about sleep, movement and other body signals.
cards.whyItMatters: Wearables show the full data pipeline in everyday life: sensors collect signals, software processes them, and algorithms turn them into information a person can use. That also makes accuracy and privacy important design questions.

csp.connection: Wearable devices collect physical-world data that software stores, processes and presents to users.

cards.headline: A new undersea cable aims for one petabit per second
cards.summary: Meta announced Petal, a planned 7,000-kilometer cable between the U.S. and France that it says will carry one petabit of data per second when it enters service in 2029. The design uses multi-core fiber to double the capacity of today's leading transoceanic cables without a proportional increase in infrastructure.
cards.whyItMatters: The internet feels wireless, but continents are connected mostly by fiber-optic cables on the ocean floor. Faster links increase how much data distant networks can exchange at once.

csp.connection: Internet data travels through physical network infrastructure, including fiber-optic links connecting continents.

cards.headline: Perseverance finds a complicated record of ancient Martian water
cards.summary: NASA says rocks examined by the Perseverance rover near the edge of Jezero Crater preserved evidence of a surprisingly complex history of water. Scientists expected sedimentary rock there but instead found igneous rock whose minerals recorded multiple episodes of water activity.
cards.whyItMatters: A rover is a remote computer-and-sensor system doing science millions of kilometers away. Its measurements become data that researchers on Earth use to reconstruct environments that disappeared billions of years ago.

csp.connection: Sensors collect observations that scientists process and analyze to infer properties of places humans cannot directly visit.

cards.headline: Decades of satellite data reveal a shift in Arctic melting
cards.summary: A NASA-led study using satellite observations from 1979 through 2023 found that the Arctic sea-ice melt season became about 40 days longer overall, but its length has been relatively stable since around 2010. Researchers say thinner ice now makes year-to-year weather patterns more influential.
cards.whyItMatters: Long-running datasets can reveal patterns that a single measurement cannot. Satellites repeatedly collect comparable data, letting algorithms and scientists study how a system changes over decades.

csp.connection: Large datasets gathered consistently over time can be analyzed to identify trends, variability and changes.

cards.headline: Students turn engineering projects into football-game technology
cards.summary: University of Central Florida students have built game-day inventions including T-shirt launchers, a robotic mascot spaceship, a customized golf cart and a projection spotlight. The projects grew from engineering labs and senior design work into equipment used or planned for UCF football events.
cards.whyItMatters: Computing and engineering do not have to start with a giant world-changing idea. Student projects can combine code, electronics, mechanics and iteration to make a familiar experience more fun or useful.

csp.connection: Students can design, prototype and improve computing-related products for real users and real settings.
